intro: Chrome live captions stop working when the speech recognition model hasn't downloaded, when Chrome needs updating, or when an extension is blocking the audio pipeline. The error message 'Live Caption is not available right now' is the most common symptom — it usually appears on Windows 10 and macOS when Chrome can't access the on-device recognition model. This guide covers the eight most effective fixes, ordered from fastest to most involved, and explains when switching to a dedicated Chrome caption extension like LessonScriptor is the better long-term solution.

sections.h2: Why have my Chrome live captions stopped working?
sections.body:
Chrome live captions stop working for one of eight reasons: an outdated Chrome version, a missing or corrupted speech recognition model, a conflicting browser extension, audio that isn't actually playing in Chrome (for example the Zoom desktop app), a corrupted Chrome profile, disabled experimental flags, insufficient disk space to store the model, or a network that blocks the model download (university or corporate firewall, VPN).

The 'Live Caption is not available right now' error on Windows 10 and Windows 11 is most often caused by the speech recognition model failing to download. Chrome downloads this model silently in the background when you first enable Live Caption — if your internet was slow or interrupted during that download, the model is incomplete and captions won't work.

On macOS, the most common cause is Chrome not being fully relaunched after an update. Another trap: Chromium-based browsers such as Brave or Vivaldi don't always include Live Caption, which is a Google Chrome feature.

The fix for 80% of cases is covered in Fix 1 and Fix 2 below.

sections.h2: Live Caption troubleshooting checklist: what to check first
sections.body: Live Caption troubleshooting starts with five checks that take under two minutes, and together they resolve most cases before you need any of the fixes below. Work through them in order: each one rules out a different cause.

steps.detail: Open **chrome://settings/accessibility** and confirm the Live Caption toggle is on. Chrome sometimes turns it off after an update.
Go to **chrome://settings/help**. Live Caption needs a current desktop Chrome on Windows, macOS, Linux or ChromeOS.

steps.strategy: Has the speech model finished downloading?
steps.detail: Right after you enable it, Chrome shows 'Downloading speech recognition files'. Captions stay blank until that finishes. A stalled download is the usual cause of 'Live Caption is not available right now'.
Check the caption language under Live Caption settings. If the video is in a language Chrome doesn't caption, nothing appears.

steps.strategy: Is audio actually playing in Chrome?
steps.detail: Live Caption only captions audio from Chrome itself, not from the Zoom desktop app or Spotify. Unmute the tab and make sure the sound isn't routed to a device Chrome can't see.

callout.label: Still blank after all five?
callout.body: Move on to Fix 1 below. If the fixes keep failing, an extension that captures tab audio directly, such as LessonScriptor's AI mode, sidesteps the speech-model download entirely.

sections.h2: Fix 1: Toggle Live Caption off and back on
sections.body:
Toggling Chrome's Live Caption setting off and on again forces the browser to reload the speech recognition model and clear any corrupted state. This resolves the majority of 'not available' errors.

**How to do it:**
1. Open Chrome and go to **chrome://settings/accessibility**.
2. Find 'Live Caption' and turn the toggle OFF.
3. Wait 10 seconds — do not close Chrome.
4. Turn the toggle back ON.
5. Close all Chrome windows completely and relaunch.

If captions now appear, you're done. If not, proceed to Fix 2.

sections.h2: Fix 2: Update Chrome to the latest version
sections.body:
Chrome's Live Caption feature requires Chrome 89 or later, and an outdated version is the second-most-common cause of captions failing, especially on university- or company-managed computers that block automatic updates.

**How to check your Chrome version:** Open Chrome → three-dot menu → Help → About Google Chrome. Chrome will check for updates automatically on this screen.

After updating, restart Chrome completely (not just close the tab — quit the application entirely and reopen). Many users report that this alone fixes persistent 'Live Caption not available' errors that had lasted for weeks.

sections.h2: Fix 3: Re-download the speech recognition model
sections.body:
Chrome's Live Caption relies on an on-device speech recognition model stored locally: Google says all audio and captions are processed locally and never leave your device. If this model is corrupted or incomplete, captions fail silently. You can force Chrome to re-download it.

**Method 1, from settings:**
1. Turn off **Live Caption** in **chrome://settings/accessibility**.
2. Under **Manage languages**, remove your caption language, then use **Add languages** to add it back. Chrome downloads the language pack again.
3. Turn Live Caption back on and restart Chrome.

**Method 2, from components:** go to **chrome://components**, find the speech recognition component (listed as 'Speech On-Device API' / SODA plus its language packs, depending on your Chrome version) and click **Check for update**. Allow 2–5 minutes on slower connections.

This is particularly effective if the error appeared after switching to a new Wi-Fi network or after Chrome auto-updated. On a filtered campus or corporate network, do the download from another connection, such as your phone's hotspot.

sections.h2: Fix 4: Disable extensions that block scripts or audio
sections.body:
Browser extensions that intercept page scripts or modify audio — including uBlock Origin, Privacy Badger, NoScript, and some VPN extensions — can prevent Chrome's Live Caption from accessing the audio stream on certain pages.

**How to test this:** Open Chrome in Incognito mode (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows, Cmd+Shift+N on Mac). By default, most extensions are disabled in Incognito. If Live Caption works in Incognito but not in regular Chrome, a conflicting extension is the cause.

**How to fix it:** Go to **chrome://extensions**, disable extensions one at a time, testing Live Caption after each until you find the culprit. For uBlock Origin specifically, you can whitelist the pages where you need captions rather than disabling the extension globally.

sections.h2: Fix 5: Chrome live captions not working with headphones
sections.body:
Chrome's built-in Live Caption works normally with headphones, including Bluetooth headphones and AirPods: it captions the audio Chrome itself plays, inside the browser, and never listens through the microphone. If captions disappear when you plug in headphones, the cause is almost always something else.

**What to check:**
- Is the audio coming from Chrome? A lecture in the Zoom or Teams desktop app isn't captioned by Chrome; open the meeting or recording in the browser instead.
- Is the tab muted? Right-click the tab > Unmute site.
- Did a Bluetooth reconnect interrupt playback? Disconnect and reconnect the headphones, then replay the video.
- Is the speech model complete? Repeat Fix 3.

**The real headphone trap:** tools that listen through the microphone don't work with headphones, because the mic can't hear audio that goes into your ears. That includes LessonScriptor's free mode, which uses the browser's speech recognition via the mic. To transcribe with headphones in LessonScriptor, use AI mode, which captures the tab's audio directly.

Chrome's **chrome://flags** page contains experimental settings that override default browser behavior. If you or a system administrator has modified flags related to audio, accessibility, or speech recognition, these can conflict with Live Caption.

**How to reset all flags:** Go to **chrome://flags** → click 'Reset all to default' in the top right → relaunch Chrome when prompted.

This is a blunt fix but effective. The only downside is it resets any other experimental flags you may have enabled intentionally.

sections.h2: Fix 7: Clear Chrome cache and browsing data
sections.body:
A corrupted browser cache can prevent Chrome's Live Caption component from initializing correctly. Clearing cached data forces Chrome to rebuild its local state.

**How to do it:** Go to **chrome://settings/clearBrowserData** → select 'All time' as the time range → check 'Cached images and files' and 'Cookies and other site data' → click 'Clear data'.

Note: this will log you out of websites. After clearing, re-enable Live Caption in **chrome://settings/accessibility** and test.

sections.h2: Fix 8: Switch to LessonScriptor if built-in captions keep failing
sections.body:
Chrome's built-in Live Caption is convenient but limited: it shows two lines that then disappear, with no way to edit, highlight or export the text. If you've tried all seven fixes above and captions still don't work reliably, a dedicated Chrome extension is the better long-term choice.

LessonScriptor is a Chrome extension that shows a live transcript in a side panel while the video plays: lecture recordings on Moodle, Canvas or Panopto, YouTube, Coursera and Udemy, and Zoom or Google Meet in the browser. The transcript is a note editor: highlights in 5 colors, bold, headers, bullets, deleting parts, slide screenshots, and export to .txt or .md. It supports 14 languages including French, Spanish, German, Portuguese and Chinese.

There are two modes. **Free mode** uses the browser's speech recognition through the microphone, so it needs speakers at a high volume (80%+) and does not work with headphones. **AI mode** captures tab audio, works with headphones and handles accents and jargon much better; it's pay-as-you-go with one-time packs and no subscription (5h for $5, 15h for $12, 30h for $21), with a 30-minute free trial.

sections.h2: Should I use Chrome's built-in captions or a Chrome extension?
sections.body:
Chrome's built-in Live Caption is best when you need quick, temporary captions and don't need to save or edit the transcript. It requires no installation, works offline once the model has downloaded, supports 19 caption languages, and works with headphones.

A dedicated Chrome extension like LessonScriptor is better when you need an editable, exportable transcript to study from, when you want to annotate a recorded lecture, or when you want higher accuracy on accents and jargon with AI mode.

The two approaches are complementary. Many users keep Chrome's native captions as a quick fallback and use LessonScriptor for serious study sessions where they need to annotate, highlight, and export their notes.

items.q: Why does Chrome say 'Live Caption is not available right now'?
items.a: This error means Chrome's on-device speech recognition model hasn't downloaded or has become corrupted. Turn Live Caption off, remove and re-add your language under Manage languages to force a re-download, or use 'Check for update' on the speech component in chrome://components. Then restart Chrome.

items.q: Do Chrome live captions work offline?
items.a: Yes, once the speech recognition model has downloaded. Chrome's Live Caption processes audio entirely on-device — nothing is sent to Google's servers. However, the initial model download requires an internet connection.

items.q: Why do Chrome live captions not work on some websites?
items.a: Some DRM-protected players, such as those of streaming services, may not let Chrome's caption engine access the audio. The feature also needs an up-to-date Chrome and a complete speech model. LessonScriptor may hit the same limitation on protected content.

items.q: Do Chrome live captions work on Chromebook?
items.a: Yes. ChromeOS has its own Live Caption feature: Settings > Accessibility > Manage accessibility features > Audio and captions > Live Caption.

items.q: Can I get Chrome live captions in French or Spanish?
items.a: Yes. Chrome's Live Caption supports 19 caption languages, including French, Spanish, German, Portuguese, Italian, Japanese, Korean, and Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Add your language under Manage languages in the Live Caption settings (chrome://settings/accessibility). If you need an editable, exportable transcript, LessonScriptor also supports 14 languages.

summary.heading: Chrome live captions not working: the short version
summary.body: Chrome live captions fail for eight reasons, and most are fixable in under five minutes. Start with the checklist, then toggle the setting (Fix 1), update Chrome (Fix 2), and re-download the speech model (Fix 3): these three steps resolve the majority of cases. Headphones are almost never the cause, because Live Caption captions Chrome's own audio without using the microphone. If you need a transcript you can keep, highlight and export, LessonScriptor adds a live transcript panel to YouTube, Zoom recordings, Canvas, Coursera and any other video in Chrome, in free mode via the microphone or in AI mode via tab audio.
